clinicalPearls: Consider WM in an older adult with fatigue, weight loss, and an incidental monoclonal IgM spike on protein electrophoresis.
Hyperviscosity symptoms (visual blurring, headache, mucosal bleeding, dizziness) reflect the very large size of the pentameric IgM molecule rather than tumor burden alone.
Bone lesions are characteristically absent, unlike multiple myeloma, which helps distinguish the two at the bedside.
Peripheral neuropathy (often demyelinating, anti-MAG antibody mediated) can be a presenting or dominant feature.
Cold agglutinin disease and cryoglobulinemia are important IgM-related complications that can cause hemolysis or vasculitis-like skin findings.
Bone marrow involvement by small lymphoplasmacytic cells with a mast-cell-rich infiltrate is a classic morphologic clue.
MYD88 L265P mutation is present in the great majority of cases and is a useful diagnostic and prognostic marker.
Asymptomatic patients with low IgM levels can often be observed without treatment (watch-and-wait).
harrison.pathophysiology: Waldenström macroglobulinaemia is a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma in which clonal B-lymphoplasmacytic cells infiltrate the bone marrow (and sometimes lymph nodes and spleen) and secrete large quantities of monoclonal IgM. The pentameric structure of IgM raises serum viscosity disproportionately to its molar concentration, producing the hyperviscosity syndrome, and the paraprotein may also deposit in nerves, precipitate in the cold (cryoglobulinemia), or bind red cells (cold agglutinin disease). Somatic activating mutations in MYD88 (and often CXCR4) drive NF-κB signaling and are central to disease pathogenesis.
additionalDifferentials: Multiple myeloma (IgM myeloma is rare but distinguishable by lytic bone lesions and different marrow morphology)
IgM monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS)
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia / small lymphocytic lymphoma
Marginal zone lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation
Other B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphomas with paraproteinemia
Amyloidosis (AL) presenting with neuropathy and paraproteinemia
nonInfectiousMimics: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) unrelated to paraproteinemia
additionalInvestigations: Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation — identifies and characterizes the monoclonal IgM spike
Serum viscosity — quantifies hyperviscosity risk when symptomatic
Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy with immunophenotyping — confirms lymphoplasmacytic infiltration
MYD88 L265P mutation testing (allele-specific PCR) — supports diagnosis and distinguishes from other lymphomas
CXCR4 mutation testing — informs prognosis and response to certain targeted therapies
Complete blood count — assesses cytopenias from marrow infiltration
Anti-MAG antibody testing — when peripheral neuropathy is present
CT imaging of chest/abdomen/pelvis — evaluates lymphadenopathy and organomegaly
redFlags: Visual disturbance, headache, confusion, or mucosal bleeding suggesting hyperviscosity syndrome requiring urgent plasmapheresis
Evidence of cryoglobulinemia with skin ulceration, digital ischemia, or renal involvement
Cold agglutinin-mediated hemolysis with severe anemia
Marked cytopenias suggesting extensive marrow replacement
Transformation to a more aggressive (diffuse large B-cell) lymphoma
pitfalls: Attributing an incidental IgM paraprotein to benign MGUS without adequate marrow and clinical evaluation when other features are present
Delaying plasmapheresis in symptomatic hyperviscosity while awaiting definitive chemoimmunotherapy
Missing WM as a cause of unexplained demyelinating peripheral neuropathy in older adults
Confusing WM with IgM myeloma or misinterpreting lytic bone lesions as consistent with WM (they are not typical)
harrison.prognosis: The disease course is typically indolent with survival often measured in many years, and asymptomatic low-burden disease can be observed safely. Prognosis is influenced by age, cytopenias, beta-2-microglobulin level, and genetic features such as CXCR4 mutation status, with most patients eventually requiring treatment for symptomatic progression.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Chapter on Plasma Cell Disorders and Waldenström Macroglobulinemia
management: Observe asymptomatic patients with a watch-and-wait approach, as low-burden disease needs no treatment and therapy is triggered by symptoms
Treat symptomatic hyperviscosity as an emergency with plasmapheresis to rapidly lower circulating IgM before or alongside systemic therapy
Initiate systemic therapy for symptomatic disease with rituximab-based chemoimmunotherapy such as bendamustine-rituximab or a cyclophosphamide-dexamethasone-rituximab regimen
Use a Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor such as ibrutinib or zanubrutinib, particularly in MYD88-mutated disease, taking CXCR4 status into account
Avoid single-agent rituximab in hyperviscous patients because of the risk of an IgM flare

Monitor the IgM paraprotein, serum viscosity, full blood count and beta-2-microglobulin, and manage IgM-related complications such as anti-MAG neuropathy, cold agglutinin haemolysis and cryoglobulinaemia
Refer to haematology for treatment selection and consider clinical-trial enrolment
